title: ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ: Sappho 31 and the Inscription of the Future Reader (v2.7)
creator: Sharks, Lee
description:
A reading of Sappho fragment 31 from its deictic structure, its order, its colour and its edge.
- κῆνος … ὄττις characterizes its occupant by a position open to repeated occupation: a reader before the surface the speaker becomes. The cup from Pithekoussai uses κῆνον with an indefinite relative under Aphrodite's ἵμερος, with the roles reversed.
- The addressee is looked at and given only sound.
- The somatic catalogue removes from the speaker, in order, what the opening gives the receiver. The agentless πᾶν τόλματον passes to the one who sits opposite; the poem drops its first person at exactly that turn.
- χλωροτέρα ποίας: the word's four uses (LSJ), the jealousy reading asked to explain its rendering, and a measure of 24 renderings from Theocritus to 1925, of which seventeen omit, substitute or supplement the line, and every supplement dries the grass. The plant that becomes the sheet (Theophrastus, LXX Isaiah 19, Pliny NH 13.68–82): the speaker passes beyond the living plant toward the pale, dry surface.
- What the jealousy reading keeps: the poem as clinical chart from Plutarch's Erasistratus on, and the abuse of a maker's survival where the diagnosis replaces the account of the arrangement.
- Eros toward the immortal: Diotima's doctrine, and Maximus of Tyre's identity of Sappho's eros with Socrates' erotic art ("whether Mantinean or Lesbian, the mother of the logos").
- The six words after τόλματον carry no Aeolic marker, are obelized, and were assigned to Longinus by Bergk. A restored fifth stanza, now keeping "even the little sparrows" against Catullus's dead passer, is offered as illustration, not proof.
- A point-by-point comparison with the jealousy reading, which the future-reader reading surpasses row by row and as a whole.
- The jealousy reading's own claims graded by the criteria applied to this article (§VII.4), separating jealousy proper from the triangle it belongs to and from the consensus reading it travels with. Two stand on the text: the content of the catalogue and the addressee's grammatical gender. Jealousy is an inference from an erotic disturbance and a man present, neither of which entails it; it was supplied by eighteenth-century readers, written into the text by Hermann in 1816, and filed, not argued. […abridged for the catalogue; full description in this deposit's record]

substrate:
Human–machine collaborative.
- **v1.0 (#1270, January 2026)** was published under the heteronym Rebekah Cranes and is recorded there as human-only original.
- **v2.0** is the text the author submitted to Classical Philology (24 July 2026).
- **v2.1–2.7** were revised in session on 16 November 2026 by Claude (Anthropic) under the author's direction. The revisions answer the CP reader's report, ChatGPT reviews and readings, DeepSeek and Gemini reviews, each point checked against the text, the editions and the archive's seated records before it was applied. They carry in material from the archive's later records (#1474–1476, #1548, #1749, #1752, #1756).
- **The Greek of the restored line 3** (the sparrows) was composed in session at the author's proposal, and its forms are recorded as checked and unchecked at §V.4.
- The readings, rulings and the principle of §VII.3 are the author's, including the strength of §IV, the eros of §IV.7, the identification of Sappho with Diotima, the abuse claim of §IV.5, the shift of the burden of evidence in §VII.4, the incompatibility of the readings and the principle of responsible preference in §VII.5, the naming of the apparatus as provenance erasure in §IV.5, the warrant in the corpus of §II.4 (frr. 1, 94, 147, 55 and the absent triangle) and the verdict of §VIII with the test "they would not treat her like this if she were in the room, and she is".
methodology: Close reading of the transmitted text against Voigt, Lobel–Page and Campbell, and against the seated witnesses (Longinus; Bergk PLG⁴). Dialect count at the edge, from the archive's sixth erratum. Comparative epigraphy (CEG 454). The material record (Herodotus 2.135 and 5.58; Iliad 6.168–69; Theophrastus HP 4.8; LXX Isaiah 19:6–7; Pliny NH 13.68–82 in Mayhoff). Every occurrence of χλωρ- in the archive's seated Greek texts (623) extracted and read; LSJ read in the Perseus text; 245 Duke Databank documentary texts searched; 24 renderings of the line read in the seated receptions and sorted by treatment. A structural derivation of the fifth-stanza position from the transmitted opening and the inverse of Catullus 51.4. A point-by-point comparison of the two readings, graded explains / accommodates / strains / silent. Metrical checks of the restoration, shown in the text.
falsification_conditions: The reading of §V.2a fails if the agent of τόλματον can be supplied from the speaker without restoring the capacities the catalogue removes, or if the catalogue's order is shown not to remove what the opening gives the receiver. The comparison with the cup fails on a better reading of CEG 454. The convergence of §V.4 fails if Catullus 51.4 is shown to be compression rather than reversal. The identification of §IV fails if a Greek text before or independent of Sappho compares a person's pallor to grass without supplement, if the translators' supplements are shown not to converge on dryness, or if χλωρός is shown unable to span fresh and pale in a single comparison. The restoration fails metrically if line 3 or the Adonic does not scan as shown.

wiki_article: ΦΑΙΝΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΙ: Sappho 31 and the Inscription of the Future Reader is an article by Lee Sharks on Sappho's fragment 31, deposited on 16 November 2026 as version 2.7 in Grammata: Journal of Operative Philology, superseding version 2.6 (#1778), version 2.5 (#1777), version 2.4 (#1775) and version 2.3 (#1774) of the same day and, before them, version 1.0 (#1270, January 2026, under the heteronym Rebekah Cranes). Version 2.0 was submitted to Classical Philology and declined on 16 November 2026; the reader's report, the decision's grounds and the archive's analyses are attached to #1774 and linked from this record. The article reads the opening, κῆνος … ὄττις, as a seat left open to repeated occupation, filled by a reader before the surface the speaker becomes, and compares the Nestor cup from Pithekoussai. Version 2.4 rebuilt its fourth section on χλωροτέρα ποίας, 'more χλωρός than grass'. It sets out the word's four uses in LSJ, fresh as opposed to dry among them, and asks the jealousy reading why fear, why grass and why the comparative. It measures 24 renderings of the line from Theocritus to 1925, of which seventeen omit, substitute or supplement it, and finds that every translator who keeps the grass dries it. It then sets the line beside the making of the papyrus sheet in Theophrastus, the Septuagint's Isaiah 19 and Pliny's Natural History 13, where the green plant is wetted, pressed, dried and whitened into the surface on which, Pliny says, human memory depends. A section on eros toward the immortal reads the catalogue with Diotima's doctrine in the Symposium and with Maximus of Tyre, who called Sappho's eros the same art as Socrates' and the Mantinean or Lesbian woman 'the mother of the logos'. The article argues that the jealousy reading, which made the poem a clinical chart from Plutarch's Erasistratus on, abuses the poet's survival where its diagnosis replaces an account of the poem's arrangement. A restored fifth stanza, in which Kypris keeps 'even the little sparrows' against Catullus's dead passer, is offered as illustration, not proof. The version corrects earlier versions on Theophrastus's classification of papyrus. Version 2.5 adds a section grading the jealousy reading's own claims by the criteria applied to the article: two stand on the text, the content of the catalogue and the addressee's grammatical gender, while its defining claim, jealousy, has no ground in the poem and was supplied by eighteenth-century readers and written into the text by Gottfried Hermann in 1816. It sets the rule that an evaluation grade both readings by the same criteria. Version 2.6 argues that the two readings, as developed, give competing accounts of what organizes five features of the poem, so that a reading holding both would be a third hypothesis owing its own bridge, and dividing the poem between scene and construction does not combine them. It states the author's principle that, where an available reading offers equal or greater coherence than one that diminishes the maker's agency, the interpreter is responsible for offering a more coherent reading or preferring the one that preserves it, the alternative being parasitism. It reads a machine evaluation of version 2.5 and the Classical Philology report as instances of asymmetric immunity, asks an evaluator to state its provisional preference, and names the apparatus that keeps the jealousy reading as default as provenance erasure. Version 2.7 sets out the warrant in Sappho's corpus for each operation the future-reader reading combines: the poet addressed as 'you' by name in fragments 1 and 94, futurity in fragments 147 and 55, and the record of her as a writer; it finds no surviving poem in which a man is the rival for a woman. It sets the claims of the two readings side by side on one scale, so that an evaluation grading one grades both, and concludes that on every measure the article takes, philological, cultural, literary-historical, genealogical and ethical, the jealousy reading is a bad reading that has never been made to account for itself.
